papers.title: High-temperature Gibbs states are uniformly Markovian and trivial
papers.abstract: We prove that, above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI). Specifically, we prove exponential decay of the CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ which need not comprise the entire system, thereby establishing a \textit{uniform Markov property} for high-temperature Gibbs states. A central obstruction to proving such bounds is that conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge due to noncommutativity. Our main insight is to construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state using an overcomplete basis. Although such representations generally involve negative quasiprobability weights, we show that a decomposition based on projective 2-designs admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperatures, allowing us to circumvent the obstruction. The separability of high-temperature Gibbs states is a natural byproduct of this decomposition. Finally, in the context of mixed-state phases of matter, our results imply that high-temperature Gibbs states belong to the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.

papers.title: Local velocimetry for atomic superfluids: from Riemann rarefaction waves to quantized vortices
papers.abstract: We demonstrate local velocimetry for atomic superfluids in two dimensions (2D). Using matter-wave interferometry based on Raman--Bragg beam splitters, we map the local gradient of the phase of the superfluid's wavefunction onto displacement of the interference fringes and reconstruct the 2D velocity field. We illustrate the capabilities of this technique by applying it to two canonical problems. First, we directly observe the self-similar evolution of the velocity field in 1D Riemann rarefaction flows. Second, we map out the full 2D velocity field around quantized vortices, explicitly demonstrating the quantization of velocity circulation.

papers.title: Query-Optimal Quantum Minimum Finding from Numerical Estimators
papers.abstract: We propose a quantum minimum-finding algorithm for objectives accessed via numerical estimators that avoids the logarithmic query overhead of amplifying the confidence of estimates before the search. A coherent estimator that is $\varepsilon$-accurate with probability at least $2/3$ on each of $N$ labels suffices to find a $2\varepsilon$-optimal label using $O(\sqrt N)$ base-estimator queries at constant confidence. The query bound and the additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. More generally, suppose a preparation assigns probability mass at least a known $p$ to objective values at most $a$. Without knowing $a$ or the prepared distribution, our algorithm returns a candidate and an estimate $v$ such that, jointly with constant probability, $v$ is $\varepsilon$-accurate for the candidate and $v\le a+\varepsilon$. The algorithm uses $O(p^{-1/2})$ queries to each of the preparation and estimator oracles in the worst case, and the selected candidate can be retained as a quantum state. For preparation width $s_P$ and estimator workspace width $w$, it requires $O(s_P+w+\log\log(4/p))$ qubits, independently of the requested confidence. Applications give worst-case optimal $Θ(\sqrt N/η)$ queries for selecting an $η$-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation using $O(ω^{-1})$ preparations and $O((ωη)^{-1})$ elementary controlled-evolution queries at constant confidence, where $ω$ is a lower bound on the guiding state's ground-space amplitude overlap.

papers.title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
papers.abstract: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates for any $ε>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

papers.title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks
papers.abstract: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of $O(N^{3/2})$ on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at $U/t=8$ and $1/8$ hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.

papers.title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
papers.abstract: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.

papers.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

papers.title: Classically Trained Quantum Generative Models with Shared Training and Fine Tuning for Quantum Matter
papers.abstract: Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter. Selected correlations can guide the classical training of a quantum sampler even when sampling the full distribution is difficult. We ask whether training across related ground-state distributions helps the sampler reproduce their correlations more accurately. We train a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram before local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, we derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with a cost that depends on the circuit generators. We also introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. We study the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model, using an automated search to select reference calculations near phase transitions. On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4 by 256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits have lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than the independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry. These results motivate shared training for preparing quantum samplers across a phase diagram and local fine-tuning.

papers.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
papers.abstract: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

papers.title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
papers.abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.

papers.title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
papers.abstract: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.

papers.title: Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model
papers.abstract: Collective two-photon light--matter interactions enable pair amplification but can destroy spectral confinement, preventing a stable thermodynamic bright phase. We show that a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction renders the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of \(N\) emitters lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized \(\mathbb Z_4\) symmetry. We determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with \(O(N^{-1})\) finite-size control and obtain the global phase diagram. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization through \(N=128\) supports the predicted density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal--bright tunneling gap. Spectral collapse thus becomes the singular zero-Kerr point of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing pair amplification.

papers.title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
papers.abstract: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.

papers.title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
papers.abstract: Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

papers.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

papers.title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
papers.abstract: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

papers.title: Tunable Ground-State Entanglement in Fully Connected Quantum Systems: From Logarithmic to Volume-Law Scaling
papers.abstract: Entanglement scaling is a central probe of the complexity of quantum many-body ground states, yet once geometric locality is absent, it can depend sensitively on the structure and normalization of interactions. For fully connected Hamiltonians with the natural Kac normalization, nondegenerate gapped ground states are known to obey a logarithmic entanglement bound. Here we ask how the ground-state entanglement changes when this interaction normalization is continuously relaxed away from the Kac scale. We answer this question by constructing an explicit all-to-all bipartite Hamiltonian of $n$ qubits with Fourier pairing amplitudes and pairwise interaction strength proportional to $n^{-κ}$. For sufficiently small fixed coupling, we prove that every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $Θ(n^{2-2κ} \log n)$ for $1/2<κ\leq1$ and $Θ(n)$ at $κ=1/2$. We further show that the ground state is unique and separated from the rest of the spectrum by a system-size-independent gap for $3/4 \leq κ\leq 1$, while weak-coupling analysis and numerical calculations suggest that the gap remains open also for $1/2 \leq κ< 3/4$. Thus, varying only the interaction normalization yields a controlled hierarchy from logarithmic scaling at the natural Kac normalization $κ=1$ to increasingly strong subextensive entanglement and ultimately to a volume law, showing that even an arbitrarily weak relaxation of this normalization precludes a universal logarithmic entanglement bound.

papers.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
papers.abstract: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

papers.title: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions
papers.abstract: Estimating the ground energy of interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum algorithms provide polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families. Classical approaches commonly rely on quantum Monte Carlo, where the sign problem is a major obstacle. However, even when a nonnegative expansion without sign problem is available, rigorous guarantees for rapid mixing are still far from well understood. In this paper, we give an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, which includes the attractive Hubbard models. This guarantee not only holds without a physical spectral gap or a weak-coupling assumption, but also covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. Technically, we first reduce ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and then use a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli and then apply the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. In addition, we obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling how many independent sampling runs and matrix updates are needed, and using sparse matrices to reduce the cost of each update.

papers.title: Imaginary-Time Density Correlations Encode Quantum Entropy and Free Energy
papers.abstract: In the classical limit, maximum-entropy inference yields an estimate of the excess entropy from the static structure factor through a single momentum sum. Quantum mechanically this estimate fails, because interactions also change the kinetic energy, while delocalization and exchange add information that equal-time correlations do not contain. We show that imaginary-time density correlations contain this information, and that with them the classical relation carries over to quantum systems. Such correlations are available from path-integral simulations and X-ray Thomson scattering. Relative-entropy inference over imaginary-time paths, with an ideal Bose or Fermi gas as reference, gives closed forms for the excess entropy and free energies, within the same Gaussian approximation as the classical relation. They recover the classical result and estimate entropy that the classical relation misses. We test them on weakly interacting bosons, interacting fermions on a ring, and the warm dense electron gas. The closed forms need only imaginary-time density correlations and their ideal-gas reference at a single state point, without using the interaction potential. Our approach can extend other classical entropy estimators to quantum systems.

papers.title: Effect of coupling asymmetry on the spontaneous decay and entanglement of two atoms in a common cavity
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics and the spontaneous decay of two identical two-level atoms into the vacuum in a cavity at low temperature. We analytically derive the survival probability and the amplitudes of the state of the system by calculating the exact self-energy when the atoms are both initially excited. It is found that moderate asymmetry enhances the decay of the survival probability and increases the entanglement production in either lossless and lossy cavities.

papers.title: Quantum Zeno Effect with a Superposed Measurement Schedule in Relational Time
papers.abstract: Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global system state is stationary, we propose a quantum circuit that explores the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom. We place two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in a coherent superposition using a schedule qubit. We show that, for a fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements taken. Then we show that, for one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, predicting a result that complements the standard Zeno probability. We propose a circuit implementation with physical memory qubits and show that measuring the memory register's joint $X$-basis parity distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one. We give the gate count and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit implementation. The Page-Wootters picture motivates this protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, although the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation. This is consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through correlations between a clock and the rest of the system.

papers.title: Entanglement, records, and quantum recovery in qubit chains
papers.abstract: We investigate entanglement, readable records and quantum recovery using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits. For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record is encoded in an off-diagonal element of the reduced density matrix and can be detected by a Pauli measurement, while a population measurement gives a higher-order signal. We further characterize the accessibility of the relative phase through joint transverse correlations and derive the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system and an accessible environment fragment. We show that interactions acting only within the environment can redistribute readable records and change the region required for quantum recovery without affecting the reduced state of the system.

papers.title: Quantum Autoencoder on Real Hardware for New Physics Searches at Muon Colliders
papers.abstract: We apply a quantum autoencoder to search for new physics (NP) in the tri-photon process $μ^+μ^-\toγγγ$ at muon colliders. Using a six-qubit circuit on the Tianyan176 quantum computer, we measure the reconstruction losses for Standard Model (SM) events and anomalous quartic gauge couplings (aQGCs) events. The results demonstrate that the hardware-implemented quantum autoencoder effectively discriminates NP signals from the SM background. Concurrently, we derive the expected constraints on the aQGCs coefficients and compare them with those obtained from conventional methods.

papers.title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
papers.abstract: How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

papers.title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
papers.abstract: Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

papers.title: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise
papers.abstract: Decomposing Hamiltonians into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. One such way of doing so is the contextual subspace decomposition, which expresses the Hamiltonian with respect to non-contextual sets of Paulis. The conditions for contextuality rely on the anticommutation and commutation of Pauli operators; it is therefore natural to make an explicit connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. Theoretical work is centered around two theorems: in the first, we consider non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and show that they are free-fermion-disguised. In the second we write these Pauli non-contextual Hamiltonians in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, showing that they carry a Jordan--Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. These two central theorems are formalized in the proof assistant language Lean. We use this to describe the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians, and highlight their relation to the more general class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. We further develop a heuristic algorithm to find line-graph based free-fermion fragments and their connected components of molecular Hamiltonians. We benchmark our algorithms against non-contextual searches for encoded molecular Hamiltonians and find comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components. Our work has implications for what fragments to consider as useful for quantum simulation.

papers.title: A Tensor-Algebraic No-Go Theorem for High-Dimensional Photonic Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger States Discovered with AlphaProof Nexus
papers.abstract: Photonic GHZ states generated with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs. In this representation, conditioning on an event with one photon in every detector turns the output amplitudes into coherent sums over perfect matchings, and generating an \(N\)-photon \(D\)-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. Here, we prove that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even \(N\ge4\) when \(D\ge N\). The proof, discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using AlphaProof Nexus, constructs a weighted sum \(\mathcal F\) of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex. Summing over the colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an \((N-1)\times N\) matrix of effective edge weights. For the graph amplitudes \(ω\) and GHZ target \(Δ\), the row--column imbalance yields \(\mathcal F(ω)=0\) but \(\mathcal F(Δ)\neq0\), contradicting the required equality \(ω=Δ\). Finally, we give a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered mathematical proof.

papers.title: Fast extraction of universal data from temporal spectrum: Applications to Haagerup CFT and monopole scattering
papers.abstract: Extracting precise universal data on conformal field theory (CFT) on the lattice traditionally requires large-scale simulations of the ground states and excitations of critical systems. Here, we propose an alternative accurate and fast algorithm, where we read off the CFT spectrum from the transfer matrix spectrum of an infinite matrix product state after a short imaginary-time evolution. We apply this method to extract the charge-resolved spectrum of a Haagerup CFT to higher levels and obtain a central charge $c = 2.137(27)$. Moreover, we show that the Maldacena--Ludwig monopole boundary can be realized as the ground state of the Fidkowski--Kitaev Hamiltonian after space-time rotation.

papers.title: Efficient calculation of the full Laguerre-Gaussian spectrum of entangled biphotons
papers.abstract: The spatial biphoton state generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enables applications in high-dimensional quantum information processing and is often described in Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes. However, calculating the full LG spectrum for arbitrary radial and orbital angular momentum (OAM) indices requires computationally demanding multidimensional integrations. We present a generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral without approximating the phase-matching function. The source geometry can be completely described by a few dimensionless parameters, which reduce to two parameters for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists. Our derived expressions for the full LG spectrum allow for computationally efficient and numerically stable evaluation at high mode orders, addressing a crucial obstacle in previous works. To illustrate our approach, we compare OAM spectra obtained by projection onto the lowest radial order and by radially insensitive detection, and investigate how high-dimensional maximal entanglement can be approached by tuning source parameters. Our results provide a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.

papers.title: A Margolus-Levitin speed limit for observables: mean energy bounds expectation-value change quadratically
papers.abstract: The Mandelstam-Tamm and Margolus-Levitin quantum speed limits bound how fast a state evolves, using the energy variance and the mean energy above the ground state. Speed limits on observables -- the change of an expectation value <A(t)> -- have so far used the variance (the Mandelstam-Tamm / quantum-Fisher-information lineage); the mean energy has not been brought to bear on the change of <A> in a fixed state. We close this branch. First, a no-go theorem: there is no state-independent linear mean-energy bound on the time to change an observable's expectation by Delta = |<A(T)> - <A(0)>|; the optimal state-independent exponent of Delta is exactly two. Second, the corresponding sharp quadratic bound, T (<H> - E_0) >= C_* Delta^2 / sigma_A^2, for every time-independent Hamiltonian H (ground energy E_0), every bounded observable A with spectral spread sigma_A = (lambda_max - lambda_min)/2, and every pure or mixed state, with the dimension-independent constant C_* = 1/(8 sin x_*) = 0.172506267461..., where x_* is the smallest positive root of tan(x/2) = x. The bound is tight, approached but not attained by a near-ground two-level family. We then give the exact energy-time/swing trade-off curve of which C_* is the small-swing slope -- tight at every swing, the observable analog of the Giovannetti-Lloyd-Maccone curve for states -- show the constant survives for mixed states via joint convexity of the trace distance, sharpen it for bandwidth-limited generators and several observables at once, and show the quadratic law degrades to a linear one when the initial state is an eigenvector of the observable. It completes the (mean-energy x observable) corner of the speed-limit landscape and, being quadratic, is most constraining where the linear variance bounds are weakest. Its cleanest physical home is the autonomous quantum clock, where it gives a coherent mean-energy resolution floor.

papers.title: Sharp State-Independent Uncertainty Relations for Multipartite systems
papers.abstract: Uncertainty relations constrain the fluctuations of incompatible observables, but most familiar bounds depend on the quantum state. State-independent uncertainty relations instead ask how much fluctuation remains unavoidable for every quantum state. For observables generated by a continuous symmetry, sharp state-independent bounds are known when the symmetry representation is irreducible. Multipartite collective systems, however, generally appear as reducible tensor-product representations of a symmetry algebra, which raises the question of how to determine their total uncertainty. We resolve this problem for multipartite quantum systems with a compact semisimple symmetry algebra $\mathfrak g$. Exploiting the symmetry structure, we formulate a general framework for state-independent uncertainty based on representation theory. The total variance admits an exact decomposition into intrinsic fluctuations within irreducible sectors and a nonnegative dispersion between sectors. This yields the sharp state-independent bound for the total variance $Δ_ρ^2(\mathfrak g)$ on the multipartite Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ \[ \min_ρΔ_ρ^2(\mathfrak g) = \min_{λ\inΛ(\mathcal H)} 2\langleλ,δ\rangle, \] where $ρ$ is any density operator on $\mathcal H$, $Λ(\mathcal H)$ is the set of highest weights $λ$ labeling those sectors, and $δ$ is the Weyl vector. This demonstrates that the ultimate uncertainty is completely controlled by its intrinsic symmetry structure. As an application of the general theory, we confirm our previous conjecture [JPA 59, 155302 (2026)] that the total uncertainty floor of collective spin-$1/2$ systems depends only on the parity of the particle number. We further illustrate the framework for multipartite spin-$1$ systems, demonstrating that the same symmetry-sector mechanism persists beyond spin-$1/2$.

papers.title: On the Four-Loop Higgs--Gluon Form Factor in Nonlocal Quantum Field Theory
papers.abstract: In particle physics the virtual N$^3$LO contribution to gluon-fusion Higgs production in the Standard Model requires four-loop multi-scale QCD amplitudes that in dimensional regularization are dominated by singular integral reduction and difficult master-integral evaluations. In this note we show that a nonlocal UV completion makes each fixed-order four-loop Feynman diagram fully convergent in four dimensions while keeping the analytic structure needed for Lehmann-Symanzik-Zimmermann (LSZ) reduction formula. For gluon-fusion $gg\!\to\!H$ we derive a closed form Schwinger-parameter representation where all loop-momentum integrals are performed analytically and thus leaving finite parameter integrals viable for direct numerical evaluation without needing the usual UV subtractions. This method heps to isolate the collider-hard contribution as a convergent four-loop form factor. The strong coupling then is defined by a finite normalization condition in the entire-function regularization scheme and it is related to the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ coupling by finite matching where after this matching, the regulator-dependent corrections decouple in the local limit $E_M\!\to\!\infty$.

papers.title: Robust Quantum Key Distribution Arbitrarily Close to Local Correlations
papers.abstract: Recently, Wooltorton et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 210802 (2024)] and Farkas [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 210803 (2024)] have exhibited the mismatch between Bell inequality violations and their cryptographic application in device-independent quantum key distribution, by showing that arbitrarily close to the set of local behaviours there exist quantum correlations guaranteeing a constant rate of secret key. While these results require correlations attaining the maximum quantum value of a suitable Bell observable (aka the Tsirelson bound) and rely on a kind of ideal self-testing of a maximally entangled state and associated Bell measurement, here we show that the effect is robust: for every one of the Bell inequalities considered by Wooltorton \emph{et al.}, a constant rate of secret key ensues if the observed Bell violation is sufficiently close to the respective Tsirelson bound. For these and also the Bell inequalities of Farkas, we furthermore present numerical results based on semidefinite relaxations of the minimum min-entropy consistent with a certain Bell violation, which demonstrate that small but nonzero key rates can be guaranteed (in principle) by practical and efficient means.

papers.title: Characterization of Chaotic Evolution in Quantum Systems Induced by Random Hermitian Matrices
papers.abstract: In a recent paper, a semiclassical Lyapunov exponent associated with a quantum Hamiltonian represented by a finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix was defined and placed on a mathematical foundation. The Lyapunov exponent characterizes the early stages of the evolution toward the ergodic state, while the late stages are characterized by the spectral gap of the corresponding Markov matrix. Here, we apply this formalism to five random-matrix ensembles. For each ensemble, we derive the mean Lyapunov exponent, its variance, and the spectral gap as functions of energy. We also present the corresponding thermal averages. Extensive numerical data are compared with the theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Fractality of the Schrödinger Density for Rough Data
papers.abstract: The observable of the Talbot effect is the intensity behind the grating: the density of the evolving field, not the field itself. Its fractality was previously known only for step data with rational jumps. We prove the general case. For arbitrary real data of bounded variation with at least one jump, the density of the free Schrödinger evolution on the torus is fractal at almost every time, with graph of upper box dimension exactly three halves. Its critical Sobolev mass diverges logarithmically, at a rate given in closed form by Wiener's jump statistic of the datum and independent of the positions and phases of the jumps. The same rate is halved along time traces and doubled for the Airy flow, so the critical mass probes the dispersion relation. Transported by the rank calculus of derangetropy operators, the theory equips every probability law with a quantum carpet: Gauss-sum revivals on quantile cells at rational times, a universal fractal at almost every other. The spectral growth rate of a single measured intensity profile returns the jump content of the grating, a prediction open to test in optical and matter-wave interferometry.

papers.title: Hydrogen Molecular Ion and Molecule in Classical Electrodynamics with Classical Zero-Point Radiation
papers.abstract: The hydrogen molecular ion and the hydrogen molecule are treated in an approximate calculation based on classical electrodynamics which includes classical zero-point radiation. It is found within the classical theory that a molecular ion is less-well bound than a hydrogen atom plus a distant proton. The smaller binding energy is explained due to the repulsive nature of the force between the proton and the atom when considering the most natural resonant orbit of the electron. The approximate classical electromagnetic calculation gives a binding energy of $2.1eV$ and a proton separation of $0.916A^{o}$ for the hydrogen molecular ion. The hydrogen molecule is formed by adding a single additional electron to the ion. The electrostatic attraction of the electron to the ion gives a binding energy of $4.6eV$ and a inter-proton separation of $0.6A^{o}$ for the hydrogen molecule in this classical electromagnetic approximation.

papers.title: Estimating the Fisher information from ARPES in general two-band models
papers.abstract: The Quantum Fisher information is frequently studied in the fields of quantum sensing and quantum metrology, as it specifies the sensitivity of a sensor through the Crámer-Rao bound, and in condensed matter physics where it relates to the quantum metric. Measuring the quantum Fisher information is therefore of significant current interest. In this work, we propose a scheme for measuring the quantum Fisher information with respect to any parameter in a general two-band solid state system using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy with carefully tuned incidence angles and light polarization. We investigate conditions under which this can be related back to information about the ground state of the material itself changing with system parameters.

papers.title: Time reversal of complex evolution on a quantum computer
papers.abstract: The Boltzmann-Loschmidt dispute in 1876-1877 discussed the problem of time reversal of ther- malization from time reversible classical equations of motion. Here, 150 years later, we highlight this problem in the frame of quantum computing. A quantum protocol is proposed that allows to perform a time reversal of complex evolution in the regime of many-body quantum chaos with many qubits. The system represents an evolution of qubits on a square lattice with inter-qubit next-nearest static couplings with a driven pulsed magnetic field. The system entropy grows rapidly to maximal values but returns to initial small values after time reversal. This time reversal is shown to be stable with respect to quantum gate imperfections. However, similar to the Lorenz butterfly effect, there is the butterfly effect of qubit when inversion of only one qubit breaks time reversibility of the whole system. It is argued that this protocol is accessible to nowadays quantum computers and annealers with hundreds of qubits.

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Hybrid Neural Networks for Neural Decoding: A Controlled Ablation Study of Learnable Quantum Sidecar Integration
papers.abstract: We study parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) integrated as residual sidecar modules within a ResNet-50 backbone for 31-class neural population decoding---imagined handwriting classification from multi-neuron spike rasters. Under strictly controlled conditions (fixed data splits, seeds, and optimizer), we compare four model variants: baseline, quantum sidecar with frozen input projection, quantum sidecar with backbone-gradient-trained projection, and a measurement-guided variant that aligns angle encodings with circuit measurement outcomes. The backbone-gradient variant improves accuracy in 3/4 seeds (+0.19% mean, 95% CI [-1.10%, +1.48%]) and consistently reduces Linear CKA similarity to baseline features ($Δ=-0.025$, 4/4 seeds), indicating genuine structural reorganization of representations. A nine-variant ablation identifies simple shallow architectures as the most effective and reproducible configuration. Measurement-guided training consistently improves representation geometry without reducing accuracy. All results use noiseless statevector simulation on 4 qubits, a regime chosen to reflect the practical constraints of current near-term superconducting hardware; no quantum computational advantage over classical methods is claimed.

papers.title: Sample-Query Interconversion of Block Encoding of Unknown Quantum States
papers.abstract: Block encoding embeds a matrix as a sub-block of a unitary matrix and serves as a fundamental input model for quantum algorithms based on quantum singular value transformation, enabling polynomial transformations of matrices encoded in unitary operators. Block encoding of unknown quantum states can be useful for quantum learning; however, the fundamental limits on converting between unknown quantum states and their block-encoding unitary channels remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate this convertibility in both directions. First, we prove that implementing an $\varepsilon$-approximate block-encoding unitary channel of an unknown quantum state requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$ copies of the state, matching known upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. Second, we show that recovering a rank-$r$, $d$-dimensional quantum state $ρ$ given query access to its block-encoding unitary channel generally requires $Ω((1/λ_{\max}(ρ))\sqrt{d/r})$ queries, where $λ_{\max}(ρ)$ is the maximum eigenvalue of $ρ$, revealing an unavoidable dependence on the dimension of the state. Our results identify inherent limitations of block encoding as a representation of unknown quantum states and reveal a separation between learning properties of a quantum state and generating the state itself. Using our techniques, we further establish lower bounds for specific state-generation tasks, including ground-state preparation and Gibbs-state preparation.

papers.title: Error Propagation Theory for Variational Non-Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics
papers.abstract: Variational approaches based on neural quantum states and physics-informed neural networks provide powerful paradigms for simulating non-Markovian open quantum dynamics. However, extending these methods into the strongly non-Markovian regime reveals a critical bottleneck: even minute errors in the time evolution can translate into substantial deviations in physical observables. The fundamental origin of this stringent precision requirement, as well as how non-Markovianity governs it, remains an open question. Here, we develop a theoretical framework that systematically characterizes error propagation in variational non-Markovian dynamics. By combining analytical derivations with numerical verification, we present the first quantitative description of variational error evolution over time. Our analysis uncovers an intrinsic error-backflow mechanism driven by long-lived environmental memory. This mechanism establishes a fundamental precision barrier and provides concrete guidance for designing robust variational algorithms for strongly non-Markovian quantum systems.

papers.title: Inclusion-Minimal local indistinguishability: a weak form of nonlocality
papers.abstract: Local discrimination of quantum states is a fundamental task in distributed quantum information processing and underlies applications such as quantum communication, data hiding, and secret sharing. Here we investigate a weak form of local indistinguishability by asking how easily it can disappear when the candidate set is reduced or an additional copy of the unknown state is supplied. We introduce inclusion-minimal locally indistinguishable sets, namely, locally indistinguishable sets for which every proper subset is perfectly distinguishable by local operations and classical communication (LOCC), and show that every finite locally indistinguishable set contains such a subset. We further find that any inclusion-minimal locally indistinguishable sets becomes perfectly distinguishable by LOCC when two identical copies are available, although a single copy is insufficient. Fininally, We construct explicit inclusion-minimal locally indistinguishable product-state sets in $(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes n}$ for every odd $d=2k+1$ and $n\ge2$. These results show that local indistinguishability can be nontrivial at the single-copy level yet fragile under either the removal of candidate states or a modest increase in copy resources, providing a complementary perspective on the structure of quantum nonlocality.

papers.title: Laughlin quasihole geometry from a single snapshot ensemble
papers.abstract: Can a probability distribution measured in one basis determine complex quantum geometry? The answer is affirmative for a lattice Laughlin quasihole. The exact occupation law at one generic reference position, together with the known analytic quasihole factor, fixes the complete complex Gram kernel. A finite snapshot ensemble estimates this kernel without preparing another member of the family, and thereby determines finite-distance overlaps, Bargmann phases, the quantum metric, and the Berry curvature. The same analytic structure confines the family to an exact projective subspace whose dimension grows at most linearly with particle number. Exact enumeration of a Nielsen-Cirac-Sierra state demonstrates finite-shot reconstruction of both the metric and a geometric phase. Moreover, a Rényi-2 divergence sets the statistical range of the reconstruction while, at nondegenerate points, occupation readout also attains the local single-copy multiparameter information bound.

papers.title: Optimal Nonparametric Estimation of Phase-Space Representations for Non-Gaussian Continuous Variable Quantum States
papers.abstract: We further develop Kernel Quantum State Estimation (KQSE), a fully data-driven nonparametric method for continuous variable quantum state reconstruction and characterization, introduced in our recent work and rooted in nonparametric kernel density estimation (KDE). Unlike approaches relying on finite-dimensional basis truncations, parametric ansätze, or prior models, KQSE combines a new kernel estimator of the characteristic function of the tomographic quadrature distribution with suitable kernel integral transformations. The characteristic function is estimated directly from experimental homodyne or heterodyne data and subsequently transformed to estimate quantum state representations and characteristics, including the Wigner function and the density matrix kernel. Observing that several other physically relevant representations and characteristics admit transformations of a closely related form, we derive convergence rates for the corresponding broad class of KQSE-based estimators. The resulting framework covers all phase-space representations, the photon-number tomogram, trace products of quantum states, and purity. We derive mean squared error convergence rates for these kernel transformed estimators and show that the corresponding KQSE applications inherit the near optimal rate O(T^{-1}), where $T$ is the total number of measurements. The proposed theory applies equally to Gaussian and non-Gaussian continuous variable quantum states without imposing a Fock space cutoff. Numerical experiments on simulated Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and real homodyne data demonstrate the advantages of KQSE over state-of-the-art methods, establishing it as a statistically consistent and computationally modest framework for continuous variable quantum state estimation and characterization, particularly in the non-Gaussian regime.

papers.title: Spinning giant optomechanical cavity with nonreciprocal self-interference
papers.abstract: We study a spinning optomechanical cavity that is coupled to a meandering waveguide at multiple spatially separated points, forming a giant-cavity configuration. The resulting self-interference makes the effective optical driving, linewidth, and frequency shift strongly dependent on the propagation phase in the waveguide, while the rotation-induced Sagnac-Fizeau shift causes the clockwise (CW) and counterclockwise (CCW) cavity modes to experience distinct interference phases. Under single-tone driving, this mechanism enables phase-controlled phonon cooling and, in the presence of cavity rotation, nonreciprocal cooling, with one propagation direction approaching the mechanical ground-state regime while the opposite direction remains less efficiently cooled. Under two-tone driving, the same interference mechanism engineers a squeezed reservoir for the mechanical mode, producing steady-state squeezing that likewise becomes nonreciprocal under cavity rotation. These results establish multi-point self-interference as a versatile mechanism for phase-controlled optomechanical reservoir engineering and show that, when combined with cavity rotation, it provides a route to nonreciprocal quantum effects.

papers.title: Relaxation-Rectified Anti-Jaynes-Cummings Cascades for Autonomous Fock-State Stabilization
papers.abstract: We propose an autonomous scheme for stabilizing prescribed Fock states in a Kerr cavity by rectifying anti-Jaynes--Cummings interactions with auxiliary-qubit relaxation. Full Lindblad simulations demonstrate steady states dominated by the Fock states $|1\rangle$ through $|4\rangle$, accompanied by pronounced Wigner negativity. An analytical birth--death model captures the steady-state populations and identifies the operating regime for stabilization. These results establish auxiliary-qubit relaxation as a resource for autonomous reservoir engineering and provide a route to nonclassical bosonic-state preparation in a single Kerr cavity and, through a boundary reservoir, in a Kerr-cavity chain.

papers.title: Engineering exact mobility edges in quasiperiodic Aharonov-Bohm chains
papers.abstract: We investigate localization phenomena and exact mobility edges in a quasiperiodic Aharonov-Bohm chain, where the 1D canonical diagonal and off-diagonal Aubry-André-Harper models are laterally coupled to an auxiliary sublattice threaded by a synthetic magnetic flux. By analytically computing the Lyapunov exponent via Avila's global theory of one-frequency Schrödinger operators, we derive exact expressions for mobility edges. In the diagonal limit, the coupling to the auxiliary sublattice generates hyperbolic mobility edges that exhibit a sign-changing divergence and can be continuously tuned by the magnetic flux. In the off-diagonal regime, the interference between quasiperiodic hopping and indirect tunneling through the auxiliary sublattice gives rise to exact anomalous mobility edges that separate critical and extended states. Critical states and anomalous mobility edges emerge even in the absence of incommensurately distributed zeros in the hopping modulation, a behavior distinct from that of conventional off-diagonal models. Our results establish a rigorous theoretical framework for engineering controllable mobility edges, with the synthetic flux providing a tunable experimental knob that paves the way for realizations in platforms such as superconducting quantum circuits and photonic waveguides.

papers.title: Bloch states of an infinite alternating-charge lattice under a transverse electric field
papers.abstract: We consider an infinite one dimensional array of alternating charges embedded in a two-dimensional configuration space and subjected to a weak static electric field transverse to the lattice axis. Expansion of the Coulomb interaction about a lattice site gives a transverse restoring stiffness $κ\propto ζ(3)/L^3$, defining the oscillator length $a_y$, while Bloch periodicity is retained along the lattice direction and the transverse motion is represented in a harmonic basis. The Coulomb matrix elements are governed by the dimensionless scale $η_{r-s}$, which couples the reciprocal-lattice transfer to the transverse oscillator length. A regularized one dimensional extension is also introduced through Coulomb regularization, yielding a finite diagonal offset and an exponentially decaying even-transfer coupling in reciprocal space. Small $η_{r-s}$ yields logarithmic, parity-dependent transverse-state coupling, while large $η_{r-s}$ approaches the one-dimensional Coulomb limit. In the finite-order spectrum, the latter approaches the Kronig Penney reference toward the band edge while retaining distinct Brillouin zone curvature. The formulation therefore identifies two characteristic quantities of the alternating lattice: the transverse restoring stiffness and the one-dimensional Madelung form, while retaining the two dimensional structure required to describe the response to a transverse electric field. Keywords: alternating charge lattice; Bloch states; Coulomb interaction; transverse electric field; regularization; reciprocal space coupling; Brillouin zone spectrum.

papers.title: Deterministic preparation of entangled Dicke states
papers.abstract: Dicke states $|J=N/2,m\rangle$ of a collection of $N$ atoms were central to Dicke's theory of superradiance. Except for the fully polarized end states, they are entangled many-body states; in particular, the single-excitation Dicke state is the W state well known in quantum information science. However, deterministic preparation of Dicke states with a prescribed spin projection remains challenging, especially without relying on postselection or heralding. Here we present a detuning-programmed Hamiltonian protocol using atoms or qubits in a dispersive cavity subject to a coherent transverse drive. In the absence of the drive, the off-resonant cavity produces an effective collective-spin interaction. By combining this cavity-mediated interaction with the coherent drive, tuning the atom--drive detuning enables the protocol, in principle, to target any allowed Dicke state along the symmetric Dicke ladder. Starting from the transverse-drive ground state, adiabatic ground-state interpolation prepares the selected Dicke state by ramping down the drive strength while ramping up the cavity-mediated interaction. After preparation, tuning the cavity into resonance with the atoms or qubits provides a direct way to probe the collective-emission response of the prepared Dicke state. We discuss implementation with superconducting circuit QED and show that the prepared states, especially the central Dicke state with $m=0$, provide resources for quantum sensing with Heisenberg-limited scaling.

papers.title: Entanglement governs early-time growth of randomness in projected ensembles
papers.abstract: Deep thermalization concerns the emergence of universal pure-state statistics in projected ensembles at late times, yet the mechanism governing the initial growth of randomness remains unclear. Here, we study the short-time dynamics of projected ensembles generated from initially unentangled states, quantifying their randomness using frame potentials. For arbitrary Hamiltonians, provided the initial bath state has full support in the measurement basis, we show that the frame potentials to cubic order in time are determined entirely by the subsystem purity, and hence by the bipartite entanglement generated between the unmeasured subsystem and its complement. The entanglement timescale therefore sets the initial timescale for the growth of local randomness, independently of the bath measurement basis. For unitarily invariant Hamiltonian ensembles, we further relate the projected-ensemble frame potential at order $k$ to the $4k$-point spectral form factor, or equivalently to the $2k$th frame potential of the global unitary dynamics, establishing a direct connection between local and global randomness. Our results identify entanglement as the mechanism governing the onset of randomness in projected ensembles and clarify how local randomness emerges from global quantum dynamics.

papers.title: Can a Local Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?
papers.abstract: In a complete quantum theory, one would construct it based on what we can observe in a system and operationally define in our universe. This philosophy goes back to some of the original ideals of quantum theory defined by W. Heisenberg, N. Bohr, and others as part of the Copenhagen school of thought. We argue in this letter that that if one wishes to construct a complete quantum field theory, that it is most natural to construct it based on a nonlocal theory of observable principles. If this interpretation is valid, then the one-particle nonrelativistic limit that recovers quantum mechanics would as well be dynamically nonlocal. In this interpretation we derive the nonlocal Schrödinger equation. We will as well demonstrate that the canonical position--momentum commutator and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle emerge from translation covariance.

papers.title: Quantum Optomechanics with Imperfect Mirrors and Casimir-Polder Effect of Atoms with Different Dynamic Polarizabilities: A Unified Treatment via a Microscopic Model
papers.abstract: This work aims at bringing the microphysics model of quantum optomechanics (QOM) proposed in [1] and developed in [2, 3] one step closer to be applicable to realistic experimental conditions, specifically, for imperfect mirrors, and for real materials. The atom/mirror-oscillator-field (AMOF) model features an internal degree of freedom for a mirror or an atom whose interaction with a quantum field determines the transmission functions of a mirror or the dynamic polarizability of an atom. We study three problems with this model: 1) An imperfect mirror moving in a cavity field, comparing results from the AMOF model with the boundary condition methods; 2) We analyze how well the dynamic polarizability derived from the AMOF model fits the tabulated data at different frequencies. 3) Combining these two parts we analyze the quantum fluctuations induced Casimir-Polder energy between a dilute atom space and a wall. We examine how well we can use the three constituent parameters of the idf oscillator in the AMOF model to match with published results on a meta-stable He* atom near a Au plate and found excellent agreements. These examples show that the AMOF model not only has a sound theoretical structure, because it is based on the microphysics dynamics of the basic constituents, it also has good practical values because it can produce accurate results for certain real materials.

papers.title: Conditional Gaussian filtering by Arthurs--Kelly readout in a three-mode cluster wire
papers.abstract: Measurement readout programs the Gaussian operation implemented by a continuous-variable cluster wire. For the standard three-node wire, momentum homodyne readout gives an additive parity channel with finite-squeezing noise. We classify the pattern-resolved input--output covariance transformations generated by calibrated uncorrelated Arthurs--Kelly readout on one or both consumed nodes. Any finite Arthurs--Kelly position record produces a conditional Gaussian filter whose gain and residual covariance depend on the input covariance entries, rather than an input-independent additive Gaussian channel. Writing $\mathrm{A}$ for Arthurs--Kelly readout and $\mathrm{H}$ for homodyne readout, the readout pattern selects the filtered sector, with $\mathrm{AH}$ selecting position, $\mathrm{HA}$ selecting momentum, and $\mathrm{AA}$ retaining both. The hierarchy $0 < τ_{\mathrm{AA}} < \min \left\{ τ_{\mathrm{AH}}, τ_{\mathrm{HA}} \right\} < 1 = τ_{\mathrm{HH}}$ shows that finite Arthurs--Kelly position records contract the gain-transferred covariance area. Our results identify calibrated uncorrelated Arthurs--Kelly readout as a measurement-level method for covariance-sensitive Gaussian filtering inside a fixed cluster graph.

papers.title: qiskit-qudits: A Qiskit Extension for Simulating Qudit Circuits
papers.abstract: qiskit-qudits is a Qiskit extension that simulates d-level qudits by encoding each one into m = ceil(log_2 d) qubits. Qudit gates are exposed as ordinary Qiskit Gate and ControlledGate subclasses, and operations that are not unitary gates (measurement, reset, barrier, state preparation) as dedicated Instruction subclasses dispatched through a dedicated apply() hook; every gate carries both a dense encoded unitary (via NumPy's array protocol) and a qubit-level definition. Because d need not be a power of two, the encoded Hilbert space is generally larger than the logical one; the library resolves this by the identity-padding convention, in which every gate acts as the identity on the unphysical part of the encoded space. When every operand dimension is a power of two, gates decompose into a fixed, transpiler-recognisable cascade of standard qubit gates; otherwise the library falls back to exact dense unitary synthesis, so that dimensions 2 <= d <= 16 are supported exactly, not only powers of two. This paper describes the software's circuit model, gate hierarchy, decomposition strategy, and measurement/decoding machinery, states its limitations, and verifies the implementation numerically: the qudit QFT against the discrete Fourier transform for both power-of-two and non-power-of-two d, extending the check of the underlying theory paper, which could only be run for d = 2^m, and every gate's emitted decomposition against its dense unitary across the whole gate set.

papers.title: A Cavity-Interfaced Register of Trapped-Ion Qubits with Multi-Second Coherence
papers.abstract: Scalable quantum networks require generating remote entanglement faster than decoherence erases it, calling for nodes that combine efficient light-matter interfaces with long coherence times. Cavity-coupled trapped ions are a promising platform for network nodes, offering high-efficiency extraction of photons. Here, we report multi-second coherence for a qubit register in a cavity-integrated ion trap. First, using dynamical decoupling on spin ground states, the coherence times of five co-trapped ion qubits are extended into the multi-second regime. Second, cavity-collected ion-photon entanglement is faithfully stored in these protected ion-memory states for multiple seconds. Third, we show that ion-memory qubits can be robust to the generation of over a thousand cavity photons by a co-trapped ion, with decoherence limited by laser crosstalk. Finally, we estimate that a modestly improved and duplicated ion-cavity system could enable the simultaneous establishment of multiple remote Bell pairs between two remote ion registers, representing a step toward networking multi-qubit prototype trapped-ion quantum processors.

papers.title: Quantifying Nonstabilizerness of Codeword-Stabilized Codes
papers.abstract: Universal quantum computation requires non-Clifford gates, which stabilizer codes can provide transversally only up to a finite level of the Clifford hierarchy. Non-stabilizer codes are not subject to this bound and are the natural candidates to fill the gap. However, it is difficult to efficiently evaluate the nonstabilizerness (or magic) of non-stabilizer codes. Here, we resolve this problem for codeword-stabilized (CWS) codes by showing that the nonstabilizerness of a CWS code is determined by the difference structure of its codewords. Whenever a Sidon set of the required size exists, the most magical codes are related to the Sidon sets, whose pairwise differences are all distinct. Structural analysis demonstrates that nonstabilizerness is invariant under coset closure, giving rise to non-stabilizer codes with arbitrarily many logical qubits and constant nonstabilizerness. Nonstabilizerness of whole code families becomes exactly computable, and we obtain closed-form values for the Kerdock codes. Moreover, we reveal a tradeoff between nonstabilizerness and transversal gates. For a code with $k$ logical qubits, a diagonal transversal gate that is non-Clifford on $t$ coordinates forces the nonstabilizerness benchmark to be at most $2(k-t)$. These results reduce the search for codes with high nonstabilizerness and for transversal non-Clifford gates to classical counting problems, to which the standard tools of additive combinatorics apply.

papers.title: Finite-Resolution Limits on Quantum Uniqueness
papers.abstract: The Stone-von Neumann theorem makes canonical quantization unique only after one imposes strong continuity of the Weyl translation groups. We show that this continuity assumption cannot be certified by any finite-resolution interrogation of the Weyl relations. A finite protocol probes only finitely many phase-space displacements and bounded expectation values, thereby determining a protocol algebra \(C_S\) generated by a finitely generated subgroup of Weyl translations, but not the regularity of an extension to the full Weyl algebra. Using the polymer representation as a canonical non-regular representation, we prove that for every regular Weyl representation, every normal state, and every finite family of bounded protocol observables, a polymer state reproduces the same expectation values to arbitrary prescribed accuracy. Thus finite agreement with Schrödinger quantum mechanics does not operationally certify the regularity hypothesis entering uniqueness. The result does not assert physical equivalence between regular and polymer quantizations, it identifies where additional input, such as Hamiltonian dynamics, energy regularity, semiclassicality, or a continuum limit, is required to distinguish or select representations. In this precise sense, non-regular polymer kinematics are not excluded by finite Weyl data alone, a point of direct relevance to quantum-gravity motivated quantizations.

papers.title: TENSKEL: A Combinatorial Observable Tensor for Structured Measurement and Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Many imaging problems seek to reconstruct underlying configurations from partial observable measurements. While reconstruction algorithms operate on these measurements, the observable organization induced by the measurement process is rarely represented explicitly.
